name: Daria Silva

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Daria. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't connected to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. Could you tell me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm foreperson at the river valley depot, in the same town I grew up in. My father worked out of that depot for thirty-four years, and some of the poles I climb, he set. We do the small towns and the farms along the valley: new connections, old poles, and a lot of trees that fall on lines. I like that when the power goes out in town, people know my truck, and they know it'll get sorted.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Changes from head office. Every year there's a new system for something, and now they want us all on some AI program for reporting. I don't use it, I write my reports the way I always have, and my supervisor grumbles but he takes them. I've got a crew to run and two kids at home, I don't need another screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised. People in the big cities get excited about every new gadget, and then the rest of us keep the lights on. I'd say that at church coffee after the service, probably.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means life carries on the way it should. My job's there, Marco's garage keeps ticking over, and the kids grow up in the same town I did. That's all I want, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing new. Keep working, keep coaching Sofia's football team on Saturdays, keep chipping away at the mortgage. We've got about two months put by, and I'd like to make that three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Content.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does chipping away at the mortgage look like for you and Marco?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco's garage has good months and bad months, so we live on my pay and put his good months on the mortgage. We don't do holidays abroad, we go camping by the lake. My kids don't know any different and they're happy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your father. What would he make of all this AI talk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd laugh, I think. He used to say a machine is only as good as the man who fixes it. He'd say the same about these computer programs.

S0.say: I'd say I'm not surprised: cities get excited about every gadget and the rest of us keep the lights on. I'd say it over coffee after church.
S0.think: I think life carries on the way it should, with my job, Marco's garage and the kids growing up in my home town. That's all I want.
S0.do: Carries on working, coaching her daughter's football team and paying down the mortgage. Aims to grow savings from about two months to three.
S0.quote: He used to say a machine is only as good as the man who fixes it.
S0.fieldNote: Daria's identity is tied to her town, her father's work and her family routines. She distrusts head office changes and the big-city excitement about technology. Her household lives carefully on her pay, with her husband's garage income as a bonus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say they should keep it in the offices where it belongs. Out here we need people who know the valley. And they'd better keep taking on apprentices, because that's how a trade survives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I worry they'd stop hiring young ones. If drones do the patrols and a machine does the tree trimming, there's no starter job for a kid from our town. That's how I started, carrying gear for my dad's crew in the summer holidays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job the way I do it. I'd put a bit extra aside, maybe fifty a week, just in case. If head office made me use a new program, I'd do the minimum and get the young lad on my crew to handle it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much, for the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said 'a kid from our town'. Is there anyone in particular you're thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My nephew, Tomas, he's seventeen and he's been asking me about apprenticeships. He's a good, steady boy who's no good at school. If this job isn't there for him, I don't know what is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if the apprenticeships dried up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The tech companies, and the people at head office who've never lived anywhere like this. They make decisions off a spreadsheet. They don't see the boy standing at the depot gate.

S1.say: I'd say keep it in the offices where it belongs, because out here we need people who know the valley. Keep taking on apprentices so the trade survives.
S1.think: I think they'd stop hiring young people if machines took the patrols and tree trimming. There'd be no starter job for a kid from our town.
S1.do: Keeps doing her job the same way and saves about fifty extra a week. Does the minimum with any new program and hands it to a younger crew member.
S1.feel: Uneasy, more for her town than herself.
S1.quote: They don't see the boy standing at the depot gate.
S1.fieldNote: Her concern in steady change is for apprenticeships and young people in her town, especially her nephew. She blames tech companies and distant head office managers. She'd do the minimum with new tools and pass them to younger workers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and I'd say it in church, at the school gate, anywhere. You can't throw a whole town's work away in two years and call it progress. I'd tell people to look after their own and look after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, it terrifies me. I'm not a computer person, I'm forty-three, and the only trade I have is this. Marco's garage might hang on a bit, but if robots fix cars too, we're both done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything: the camping trips, the kids' extras, the second car. I'd help Marco in the garage on weekends, doing the books and tyres, to build that up while my job lasts. And I'd talk to my mother and my church about how we'd all help each other if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Sick in my stomach, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to your church. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our church already runs a food bank and helps families when someone's sick. I'd want us to organise properly, for jobs and childcare, before people are desperate. I'd rather lean on my neighbours than queue at a government office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Sofia and Luca?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Mum's job is changing and we're going to be careful with money for a while. I wouldn't tell them I was scared. Kids shouldn't carry that.

S2.say: I'd say it's wrong to throw a whole town's work away in two years and call it progress. I'd tell people to look after their own and each other.
S2.think: I think it terrifies me: I'm not a computer person, I'm forty-three and this is my only trade. If robots fix cars too, both Marco and I are done.
S2.do: Cuts camping trips, the kids' extras and the second car. Helps in Marco's garage on weekends to build that income, and organises help through her mother and church.
S2.feel: Frightened and sick to her stomach.
S2.quote: I'd rather lean on my neighbours than queue at a government office.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture threatens both her job and her partner's garage. Her instinct is to turn to family, church and neighbours rather than the state, which fits her views. She'd hide her fear from her children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time for the big companies to do right by the people who built this country's power lines. Apprenticeships, keep people on, don't just chase the cheapest option. I'd vote for whoever says that and means it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd keep hoping it doesn't reach the valley. But I'd be forty-eight and still not a computer person. It'd be like watching a storm come up the river and knowing there's nowhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save every bit I could, maybe a hundred a week, and stop any home projects. I'd build up the garage side with Marco, maybe add tyre fitting so there's a second income. I wouldn't take any computer courses, I'd just be wasting their time and mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd be praying a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be wasting their time with a course. Are you sure about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've seen myself with that reporting program. I'm good at what I do because I've done it with my hands for twenty years. A classroom isn't where I learn anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would five years mean for Sofia and Luca?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sofia would be eighteen. I'd want her to find something solid, maybe nursing like my sister. Luca would still be at school, and I'd want him to learn a trade that needs a person, if there is one.

S3.say: I'd say five years is enough for big companies to do right by the people who built the power lines. Keep apprenticeships and keep people on, and I'd vote for whoever means it.
S3.think: I think I'd hope it never reaches the valley but know I'd be forty-eight and still not a computer person. It's like watching a storm come up the river.
S3.do: Saves about a hundred a week and stops home projects. Builds up the garage with Marco, adding tyre fitting as a second income, and skips computer courses.
S3.quote: It'd be like watching a storm come up the river and knowing there's nowhere to go.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives her time to build a second income through the garage, but she rules out retraining herself. Her faith is a steady support. She thinks about her children's futures in terms of solid, human work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is time to train young people properly and look after the older ones. Families and communities should be planning, not waiting for handouts. That's what I'd say at church and anywhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years almost feels worse, if I'm honest. Ten years of watching it come, every new machine on the news. I'd be fifty-three at the end and still not ready for a different life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on in my job and save as much as I can every year. I'd make sure the kids get good skills, Sofia through college and Luca into an apprenticeship if there's one worth having. We'd probably not move house or take on anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, a slow kind. Like a toothache.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years feels worse. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years you just get hit and you deal with it. With ten, you lie awake for ten years. I'd rather not know, sometimes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything the extra time would let you do that the short ones wouldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get the mortgage smaller and get the kids through school. That's real, I'll give it that. But I'd still be the same person at the end, with the same hands.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is time to train young people properly and look after older workers. Families and communities should plan rather than wait for handouts.
S4.think: I think ten years almost feels worse, ten years of watching it come. I'd be fifty-three and still not ready for a different life.
S4.do: Keeps working and saves as much as possible each year. Makes sure her daughter gets through college and her son into a worthwhile apprenticeship, and avoids new commitments.
S4.feel: A slow, ongoing anxiety, like a toothache.
S4.quote: With two years you just get hit and you deal with it. With ten, you lie awake for ten years.
S4.fieldNote: Unusually, she feels the longer warning almost as hard as the short one, because it means years of dread. She grants that the time helps with the mortgage and the children. She sees herself as unchanged at the end, which is the heart of her worry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there'd be no time to do anything. What would help is companies keeping apprenticeships going and keeping experienced people on to train them and check the machines. And help for small businesses like Marco's garage, so families have something to fall back on that isn't a handout.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the town. When the depot goes, it's not just jobs. It's the truck people wave at, and the woman whose dad set the poles.

headlineQuote: It's the truck people wave at, and the woman whose dad set the poles.
portrait: Daria Silva is a 43-year-old foreperson at the river valley depot in the town where she grew up, climbing poles her father once set. She never uses AI and hands any new program to a younger crew member. Steady change worries her mostly for the apprentices and young people in her town. The two-year AGI picture terrifies her because it would threaten both her job and her husband's garage, and she'd turn to family and church rather than the state. Oddly, she finds the ten-year picture almost as hard, because it means years of watching it come.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because there'd be no time to do anything before both her job and her husband's garage were at risk.
whatWouldHelp: Companies keeping apprenticeships and experienced staff on to train people and check the machines, and support for small family businesses so there's something to fall back on that isn't a handout.
